episode_title: Special Edition: City Income Tax Info Discussion Featuring Austin Hensley of the “Vote No Beavercreek Income Tax” Group

real_qa.q: Why did Austin Hensley move from Dayton to Beavercreek in 2015?
real_qa.r: Austin moved to Beavercreek because he discovered that Dayton had a significant income tax deduction on his paycheck. He learned that only three cities in Ohio do not have an income tax, and Beavercreek, located six miles away, was one of them. When he changed his residency and moved to Beavercreek at the end of 2015, his paycheck increased by $60 every two weeks.
real_qa.requete: Why did Austin Hensley move to Beavercreek

real_qa.q: What is the sixth income tax attempt in Beavercreek and why does Austin Hensley oppose it?
real_qa.r: The 2026 income tax proposal is the sixth attempt by Beavercreek to implement a municipal income tax, with previous attempts in 2020, 2022, and 2026. Austin opposes it because he believes that after two rejections at the ballot box, voters have expressed a democratic mandate, and the issue should die. He argues that all three recent attempts have had no substantive changes—always a property tax reduction in exchange for an income tax on workers, with the millage currently at 10 mils.

real_qa.q: How much did Beavercreek propose to raise through the municipal income tax according to the city?
real_qa.r: According to the CityZone website, the city proposed that all $19.6 million from the income tax would go into the general fund with no restrictions or specific purpose allocation, unlike property tax levies which are renewable periodically with fixed dollar amounts and fixed terms.

real_qa.q: When was Beavercreek incorporated as a city and what charter provision did its founders establish regarding income tax?
real_qa.r: Beavercreek was founded in 1980, and the founders wisely created a city charter provision that prevents any imposition of an income tax without explicit voter approval. Additionally, they placed municipal elections in odd-numbered years to lower turnout and increase participation from voters more tuned into local politics, making it easier for citizens to place ballot initiatives on the ballot.
real_qa.requete: Beavercreek chartered 1980 income tax charter provision

real_qa.q: What alternative funding mechanism does Austin Hensley propose if property taxes are eliminated in Ohio?
real_qa.r: Austin proposes a sales tax at the county level that would be applied to non-essential purchases and apportioned to cities and townships based on population. However, he acknowledges he has not done the exact math and is not a state legislator. He notes that any such change would require action by the state legislature, as sales tax is only handled at the state level in Ohio.
real_qa.requete: county sales tax alternative property tax elimination Ohio

guest.entreprise: Vote No Beavercreek Income Tax Group
guest.bio_context: Austin moved to the Dayton area in 2015 to work at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base as a GS-9 trainee in the Copper Cap program to become a contracting officer. He relocated from downtown Dayton to Beavercreek at the end of 2015, where he discovered the city had no income tax unlike Dayton. His involvement in tax policy began in 2020 when he became active in opposing municipal income tax proposals.

real_quote: We don't have to live like this. We don't have to live in a world where everything gets bogged down by red tape, permitting processes, meetings and hearings.
